# Volume 5 — CHAPTER XXII. ST. LAURENCE KNOWS ALL ABOUT IT

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

When midnight arrived, Harriet Ainslie was returning on foot to her house from the silver wedding of the Pollocks. She had remained for a short time following the departure of the remaining guests, assisting the bride with gray hair as she washed dishes. Because the space separating the pair of homes was brief and the path was in good condition, Harriet was taking pleasure in her moonlight return journey to her house.
{: #nw-v05-c22-p0000 }

The night had proved to be an enjoyable one. It was very enjoyable for Harriet, who had not attended a party in years. Every guest had belonged to her former circle, and no unwelcome young people were there to ruin the atmosphere, since the bride and groom’s only son was attending college far away and was unable to attend. Lionel Fairlie had attended, and it was the first time they had met in a social setting in years, even though she had spotted him one or two times in church during that winter. Their encounter did not stir the slightest bit of romance in Harriet’s heart. Whenever she pondered the matter at all, she was used to being amazed that she could have ever been attracted to him or been so deeply hurt by his abrupt wedding. Nevertheless, she had quite enjoyed seeing him once more. She had failed to remember how invigorating and inspiring he was able to be. An assembly was never dull whenever Lionel Fairlie was in attendance. Everyone was astonished when Lionel arrived. His habit of never going out was common knowledge. He had been asked by the Pollocks because he was among the original guests, yet they did not actually expect him to show up. He escorted his second cousin, Amy Annetta Fairlie, to supper and appeared quite attentive toward her. However, Harriet was seated opposite him at the table and engaged in a lively debate with him—a debate throughout which his entire shouting and teasing failed to fluster her, and from which she emerged victorious, defeating Lionel so calmly and thoroughly that he said nothing for ten minutes. When those minutes had passed, he growled into his reddish beard—“spunky as ever—spunky as ever”—and started picking on Amy Annetta, who laughed foolishly at his remarks where Harriet would have offered a sharp comeback.
{: #nw-v05-c22-p0001 }

These matters were pondered by Harriet as she made her way back, savoring them with a backward-looking enjoyment. Frost made the night air, lit by the moon, glisten. Beneath her boots, the snow crunched. The Glen spread out beneath her, leading to the snowy harbor past it. A lamp burned inside the manse study. John Ashdown had returned home, then. Was Clementine asked by him to be his wife? And in what manner had her rejection been communicated? That she would never learn this was Harriet's feeling, despite her considerable inquisitiveness. That Clementine would refrain from ever sharing anything regarding the matter with her was a certainty to her, nor would she have the courage to inquire. The reality of the rejection simply had to satisfy her. Ultimately, nothing else was truly important.
{: #nw-v05-c22-p0002 }

“I wish he possesses sufficient wisdom to return occasionally and act amicably,” she uttered inwardly. Her aversion to isolation was so strong that speaking her thoughts was a method she used to bypass unwanted loneliness. “It is terrible to lack a intelligent male figure to converse with on occasion. And it is quite probable he will refrain from approaching the dwelling forever. Lionel Fairlie exists as well—that individual appeals to me, and I would enjoy engaging in a spirited debate with him occasionally. However, he would not venture here lest folk suspect he was pursuing me anew—or perhaps lest I suspect it myself—even though he feels more unfamiliar to me at present than John Ashdown. The idea that we were once romantic partners resembles a fantasy. Yet that remains the reality—a mere two males in the Glen merit my conversation—and owing to rumors and this miserable romantic affair it is improbable I will behold either one henceforth. I was capable,” Harriet stated, directing her words toward the indifferent stars with bitter force, “of creating a superior world on my own.”
{: #nw-v05-c22-p0003 }

A sudden, indistinct sense of dread made her stop beside her gate. A light continued to shine in the living-room, where the silhouette of a woman paced back and forth, moving incessantly across the window-shades. Why had Clementine not gone to bed at such a late hour? And what reason did she have to march back and forth like a mad person?
{: #nw-v05-c22-p0004 }

Harriet stepped quietly inside. Clementine emerged from the room just as she unclosed the entrance to the hall. Her face was red, and she was out of breath. She was surrounded by an aura of strain and intensity as if wearing it.
{: #nw-v05-c22-p0005 }

“Clementine, what is the reason you are not sleeping?” Harriet asked.
{: #nw-v05-c22-p0006 }

“Step inside,” Clementine said with intensity. “There is something I wish to tell you.”
{: #nw-v05-c22-p0007 }

Taking off her wraps and galoshes with composure, Harriet went after her sister into the room that was warm and lit by the fire. Remaining stationary with her hand upon the table, she waited. In her own stern, dark-eyebrowed manner, she was looking quite handsome. Designed by her specifically for the gathering, the new black velvet gown, featuring a V-neck and a train, suited her grand, large frame. Wrapped about her neck, she wore the opulent, weighty amber bead necklace that served as a family relic. Her face had been bitten to a radiant red by her stroll through the crisp air. Nevertheless, her steel-blue eyes remained just as frozen and rigid as the night sky in wintertime. She remained standing and waiting in a quietness that Clementine could disrupt solely through a spasmodic exertion.
{: #nw-v05-c22-p0008 }

“Harriet, this evening Mr. Ashdown was here.”
{: #nw-v05-c22-p0009 }

“Yes?”
{: #nw-v05-c22-p0010 }

“And—and—he requested that I become his wife.”
{: #nw-v05-c22-p0011 }

“That is what I anticipated. Naturally, you turned him down?”
{: #nw-v05-c22-p0012 }

“No.”
{: #nw-v05-c22-p0013 }

“Clementine.” Harriet’s fists tightened as she unconsciously moved a step toward her. “Are you saying that you agreed to marry him?”
{: #nw-v05-c22-p0014 }

“No—no.”
{: #nw-v05-c22-p0015 }

Harriet regained control of her feelings.
{: #nw-v05-c22-p0016 }

“What was your next course of action?”
{: #nw-v05-c22-p0017 }

“I—I requested that he grant me several days to consider the matter.”
{: #nw-v05-c22-p0018 }

“I do not quite understand why that had to be done,” Harriet remarked, with aloof disdain, “since you can give him but a single response.”
{: #nw-v05-c22-p0019 }

In an imploring gesture, Clementine extended her hands.
{: #nw-v05-c22-p0020 }

“Harriet,” she pleaded, “John Ashdown has my heart—I desire to become his spouse. Would you release me from that vow?”
{: #nw-v05-c22-p0021 }

“No,” Harriet replied, lacking any pity, since terror was making her ill.
{: #nw-v05-c22-p0022 }

“Harriet—Harriet—”
{: #nw-v05-c22-p0023 }

“Listen,” Harriet broke in. “That promise was not requested by me. It was offered by you.”
{: #nw-v05-c22-p0024 }

“I am aware—I am aware. However, back then, I failed to believe I might ever love somebody else.”
{: #nw-v05-c22-p0025 }

“It was proffered by you,” Harriet continued without flinching. “Over the Bible belonging to our mother, your word was given. Rather than a mere promise, an oath was made. At present, you wish to go back on it.”
{: #nw-v05-c22-p0026 }

“Harriet, my sole request was for you to release me from it.”
{: #nw-v05-c22-p0027 }

“I shall refrain from doing it. To me, a pledge remains a pledge. I shall refrain from doing it. Violate your own word—commit perjury if you so choose—yet it will occur without any agreement from me.”
{: #nw-v05-c22-p0028 }

“Harriet, you treat me with great severity.”
{: #nw-v05-c22-p0029 }

“It is severe for you! But what about my situation? Did it ever cross your mind how isolated I would be in this place should you abandon me? That would be unbearable for me—my mind would break. Existing by myself is impossible for me. Has my sisterhood to you not been devoted? Was there ever a desire of yours that I stood against? Did I not yield to all your whims?”
{: #nw-v05-c22-p0030 }

“Yes—yes.”
{: #nw-v05-c22-p0031 }

“Why, then, is it your wish to abandon me for a man you were unacquainted with a year back?”
{: #nw-v05-c22-p0032 }

“Harriet, I am in love with him.”
{: #nw-v05-c22-p0033 }

“Love! Your speech resembles that of a school miss rather than a middle-aged woman. His feeling for you is not love. What he desires is a housekeeper and a governess. Your feeling for him is not love. Your desire is to be ‘Mrs.’—you belong to that group of weak-minded women who consider it a disgrace to be categorized as an old maid. There is nothing more to it than that.”
{: #nw-v05-c22-p0034 }

Clementine trembled. Harriet was unable, or perhaps unwilling, to comprehend. It was futile to debate with her.
{: #nw-v05-c22-p0035 }

“Then you refuse to set me free, Harriet?”
{: #nw-v05-c22-p0036 }

“No, I will not. Nor will I speak about it any more. A promise was made by you, and you must hold to your word. Nothing else needs to be said. Retire to sleep. Observe the hour! Romantic excitement has overcome you. By to-morrow, your good sense will return. In any case, I am not to hear another word of this foolishness. Go.”
{: #nw-v05-c22-p0037 }

Clementine departed in silence, her face drained of color and lacking energy. After pacing the room angrily for a short duration, Harriet stopped in front of the seat in which St. Laurence had slept peacefully all night long. An unwilling grin spread across her swarthy countenance. Harriet had failed to balance drama with humor on merely a single occasion in her existence—at the moment her mother died. Even during that distant period of grief, when Lionel Fairlie had jilted her to an extent, she had found reason to laugh at herself just as frequently as she had wept.
{: #nw-v05-c22-p0038 }

“I anticipate some pouting will occur, St. Laurence. Indeed, Saint, a period of disagreeable, misty days likely lies ahead for us. Nevertheless, we will ride them out, Laurence. Foolish youths have been managed by us in the past, Saint. Clementine will mope for a time—and afterwards she will recover from it—and everything will return to its previous state, Laurence. She gave her word—and she is required to fulfill her vow. And those are the final remarks regarding the matter that I shall utter to you, to her, or to any person, Saint.”
{: #nw-v05-c22-p0039 }

Yet till the arrival of morning, Harriet remained fiercely awake in her bed.
{: #nw-v05-c22-p0040 }

No brooding occurred, however. The following day, Clementine appeared pale and silent, yet Harriet noticed no other alteration in her behavior. Indeed, she appeared to harbor no resentment toward Harriet. Because the weather was tempestuous, no one spoke of attending church. During the afternoon, Clementine locked herself in her bedroom and composed a line to John Ashdown. She lacked the confidence to utter “no” face to face. She was entirely convinced that if he surmised her “no” was given unwillingly, he would refuse to accept it, and she lacked the fortitude for entreaties or supplications. She had to convince him that he meant absolute zero to her, a feat achievable solely through correspondence. She drafted the most formal, icy little rejection one could conceive. It was scarcely polite; it undeniably offered no faint ray of hope to even the most daring suitor—and John Ashdown was far from daring. He recoiled internally, wounded and humiliated, upon reading Clementine’s message the following day inside his dusty study. Yet beneath his humiliation, a terrible truth soon became apparent. He had believed his affection for Clementine was inferior to the love he had harbored for Cecilia. At present, having lost her, he recognized that he truly did. She represented all things to him—all things! And he was forced to remove her from his existence entirely. Even comradeship was now out of the question. Existence lay ahead of him in unbearable gloom. He was required to continue—he possessed his labor—his offspring—yet his spirit was utterly destroyed. He remained isolated the entire evening inside his dim, chilly, uninviting study, his head resting upon his hands. High on the hill, Clementine suffered from a headache and retired to bed early, whereas Harriet observed to St. Laurence, who purred his contempt for senseless humanity, who failed to realize that a plush cushion was the sole matter of genuine importance,
{: #nw-v05-c22-p0041 }

“How would women manage had headaches not been created, St. Laurence? However, it does not matter, Saint. For a short time, we shall simply close an eye to it. I allow that I do not feel at ease myself, Laurence. My sensation is like having submerged a kitten. Nevertheless, she gave her word, Saint—and the proposal came from her, Laurence. Bismillah!”
{: #nw-v05-c22-p0042 }
